FALSE DESIGNATION OF ORIGIN AND FALSE ADVERTISING UNDER LANHAM ACT § 43(A) (15 U.S.C. § 1125(A)) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Harbor Line Provisions, LLC · Packaged sauces sold online, and a competitor's advertisement comparing shelf life

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS LANHAM ACT SECTION 43(A) INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes the federal cause of action created by section 43(a) of the Lanham Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1125(a), for false designation of origin and for false advertising. It is prepared by Jordan T. Reyes for Harbor Line Provisions, LLC concerning Packaged sauces sold online, and a competitor's advertisement comparing shelf life. Section 43(a) is the Lanham Act's general unfair-competition provision, and it applies whether or not a mark is federally registered. It has two prongs. The first, 15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(1)(A), reaches a use in commerce that is likely to cause confusion or mistake, or to deceive, as to affiliation, connection, or association with another person, or as to the origin, sponsorship, or approval of goods, services, or commercial activities; passing off, reverse passing off, and false endorsement claims are brought under it. The second, 15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(1)(B), reaches a misrepresentation, in commercial advertising or promotion, of the nature, characteristics, qualities, or geographic origin of goods, services, or commercial activities. In Dastar Corp. v. Twentieth Century Fox Film Corp., 539 U.S. 23 (2003), the Supreme Court held that the "origin of goods" the first prong protects is the producer of the tangible goods offered for sale and not the author of any idea, concept, or communication embodied in them, so that copying an uncopyrighted work and selling it without credit is not by itself a section 43(a) violation. This Information Sheet states what the statute provides, what the Supreme Court and the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit — whose decisions bind the federal district courts in California — have said about it, what remedies the Lanham Act makes available, and how the parallel California unfair-competition and false-advertising statutes are worded. It is not a demand letter, not a complaint, not a determination that any statement, label, credit, or advertisement concerning Packaged sauces sold online, and a competitor's advertisement comparing shelf life violates or complies with any law, and not legal advice.

HOW THIS INFORMATION SHEET RELATES TO THIS PROJECT'S OTHER INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY DOCUMENTS
Section 43(a) supplies the statutory text for several different claims, and this project addresses most of those claims in separate documents rather than here. Infringement of a registered or unregistered word mark or logo, and the cease-and-desist letter that often precedes suit, are the subject of this project's trademark infringement cease-and-desist and trademark registration documents; the protectability and functionality of product packaging and product design under 15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(1)(A) and § 1125(a)(3) are the subject of its trade dress document; dilution of a famous mark under 15 U.S.C. § 1125(c) and the nominative and classic fair use defenses are the subject of its trademark dilution and trademark fair use materials; cybersquatting under 15 U.S.C. § 1125(d) is the subject of its domain name dispute document; and the use of a person's name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness is the subject of its right of publicity and model release documents. On the copyright side, registration and its role as a precondition to an infringement suit, the first sale doctrine, joint authorship, copyright preemption of state-law claims, what copyright does not protect, and the federal and California moral rights statutes are each covered in their own documents. What this Information Sheet adds is the structure of section 43(a) itself: the difference between its confusion prong and its commercial-advertising prong, the passing off and reverse passing off doctrines, the limit the Supreme Court placed on attribution claims in Dastar, the elements and proof of a false advertising claim, who may sue, the statutory remedies, and the California statutes that cover similar ground. This document concerning Packaged sauces sold online, and a competitor's advertisement comparing shelf life does not restate the material covered by those other documents.

THE STATUTORY TEXT: TWO PRONGS OF 15 U.S.C. § 1125(A)(1)
Section 43(a)(1) of the Lanham Act, codified at 15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(1), begins with a single set of conduct requirements and then branches into two separate prongs. The opening language applies to any person who, on or in connection with any goods or services, or any container for goods, uses in commerce a word, term, name, symbol, or device, or any combination of them, or any false designation of origin or false or misleading description or representation of fact. Subparagraph (A) then covers uses likely to cause confusion, mistake, or deception as to affiliation, connection, or association with another person, or as to the origin, sponsorship, or approval of goods, services, or commercial activities. Subparagraph (B) covers a different wrong: a misrepresentation, made in commercial advertising or promotion, of the nature, characteristics, qualities, or geographic origin of the speaker's own or another person's goods, services, or commercial activities. The text of neither prong requires that the plaintiff own a federal trademark registration, and the text of subparagraph (B) does not mention a mark at all. The closing sentence of paragraph (1) states who may be sued and by whom: the person whose use meets either prong is liable in a civil action brought by any person who believes that he or she is or is likely to be damaged by the act. The same section contains provisions this clause does not reproduce, including 15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(2) on State defendants, § 1125(a)(3) on the burden of proving that unregistered trade dress is not functional, § 1125(b) on imported goods, § 1125(c) on dilution of famous marks, and § 1125(d) on cybersquatting.

PASSING OFF AND REVERSE PASSING OFF AS NINTH CIRCUIT LAW DESCRIBES THEM
Traditional passing off is selling one's own goods as those of another. Reverse passing off is the mirror image: selling another's goods as one's own. In Smith v. Montoro, 648 F.2d 602 (9th Cir. 1981), an actor alleged that a film distributor had removed his name from the credits and advertising for a film in which he had starred and substituted another actor's name. The district court dismissed the Lanham Act claim on the ground that the conduct was not the economic equivalent of palming off. The Ninth Circuit reversed, holding that a section 43(a) claim may rest on conduct economically equivalent to palming off, and describing reverse passing off as conduct that occurs when a person removes or obliterates the original trademark, without authorization, before reselling goods produced by someone else. The court distinguished two forms. Express reverse passing off occurs when the wrongdoer removes the name or trademark on another party's product and sells that product under a name the wrongdoer chooses. Implied reverse passing off occurs when the wrongdoer simply removes or obliterates the name of the manufacturer or source and sells the product unbranded. The court described the injury as both a misappropriation of another's talents and workmanship and a deprivation of the advertising value of the originator's name and of the goodwill that public knowledge of the true source would generate.

DASTAR: "ORIGIN OF GOODS" MEANS THE PRODUCER OF THE TANGIBLE GOODS
In Dastar Corp. v. Twentieth Century Fox Film Corp., 539 U.S. 23 (2003), the copyright in a television series had expired, leaving the series in the public domain. Dastar copied the series, made modifications, and sold the result as its own video set without crediting the original. The holders of rights connected with the original series sued under section 43(a), arguing that selling the copied material without acknowledging its source was a false designation of origin. The Supreme Court reversed the judgment against Dastar. It drew a line between two situations: a claim would undoubtedly have been sustained had Dastar bought finished videotapes from the authorized distributor and repackaged them as its own, but Dastar had instead copied a public-domain work and produced its own tapes. Construing the phrase "origin of goods," the Court held that it cannot connote the person or entity that originated the ideas or communications that goods embody or contain, and concluded that the phrase refers to the producer of the tangible goods offered for sale rather than to the author of any idea, concept, or communication embodied in those goods. The consequence is that a failure to credit the creator of content that a defendant lawfully copied is not, without more, a violation of 15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(1)(A).

WHY THE COURT DREW THAT LINE: SECTION 43(A) IS NOT A SUBSTITUTE FOR COPYRIGHT
The Dastar Court explained the limit it placed on the confusion prong by reference to what the Lanham Act is for and to what the copyright and patent laws already do. Section 43(a), the Court said, prohibits actions like trademark infringement that deceive consumers and impair a producer's goodwill; its illustration was one soft-drink company passing off its product as a competitor's, or reverse passing off the competitor's product as its own. Reading the same provision to require attribution for the intellectual content of a product would, the Court reasoned, create rights that outlast the federal intellectual property statutes that govern that content, and it said that holding otherwise would be akin to finding that section 43(a) created a species of perpetual patent and copyright, which Congress may not do. The effect of that line is that the confusion prong addresses deception about who produced the physical goods a buyer receives, while a claim about the copying of the content itself arises, if at all, under copyright law, with its own requirements, defenses, and term of protection.

WHAT DASTAR LEFT OPEN: MISREPRESENTATION UNDER THE COMMERCIAL ADVERTISING PRONG
The Dastar Court distinguished the claim before it from a different claim under the other prong of the same statute. It observed that if the producer of a video that substantially copied the earlier series had given purchasers the impression, in advertising or promotion, that the video was quite different from that series, one or more of the plaintiffs might have had a cause of action — not for reverse passing off under the confusion provision of section 43(a)(1)(A), but for misrepresentation under the provision of section 43(a)(1)(B) addressing the nature, characteristics, and qualities of goods. The Court added that merely saying it was the producer of the video exposed Dastar to no Lanham Act liability. The distinction matters because the two prongs ask different questions: the first asks whether the public is likely to be confused about source, sponsorship, or affiliation, and the second asks whether a statement made in commercial advertising or promotion misdescribes what the goods or services are or what they do.

NINTH CIRCUIT APPLICATION: MISREPRESENTING LICENSING STATUS IS NOT A SECTION 43(A) CLAIM
Federal district courts in California follow the Ninth Circuit, which applied Dastar to both prongs of section 43(a) in Sybersound Records, Inc. v. UAV Corp., 517 F.3d 1137 (9th Cir. 2008). A karaoke record producer sued competitors, alleging that they had obtained fewer copyright licenses than they claimed and had therefore produced their discs more cheaply, and that their representations of compliance were actionable under the Lanham Act. The court of appeals affirmed dismissal. It read Dastar as holding that "origin of goods" in section 43(a)(1)(A) refers to the producer of the tangible good rather than to the author of any idea, concept, or communication embodied in it, and it then applied the same concern about overlap between the Lanham Act and the Copyright Act to the commercial-advertising prong: the nature, characteristics, and qualities of a recording are more properly construed to mean characteristics of the good itself, such as the original song and artist and the quality of the audio and visual effects, rather than the licensing status of the underlying copyrights. The court reasoned that a contrary reading would let nonexclusive licensees and strangers to a copyright litigate copyright infringement through the Lanham Act even though they lack standing to sue for infringement.

THE ELEMENTS OF A FALSE ADVERTISING CLAIM AND THE TWO WAYS OF PROVING FALSITY
The Ninth Circuit stated the elements of a false advertising claim under section 43(a) in Southland Sod Farms v. Stover Seed Co., 108 F.3d 1134 (9th Cir. 1997), a suit between competing sellers of turfgrass seed over advertisements comparing growth rates. The elements are a false statement of fact by the defendant in a commercial advertisement about its own or another's product; a statement that actually deceived or has the tendency to deceive a substantial segment of its audience; materiality, in that the deception is likely to influence the purchasing decision; entry of the false statement into interstate commerce caused by the defendant; and injury to the plaintiff, or likely injury, either by direct diversion of sales or by a lessening of the goodwill associated with the plaintiff's products. Falsity may be shown in either of two ways: that the statement was literally false, on its face or by necessary implication, or that it was literally true but likely to mislead or confuse consumers. The court added that an advertising claim must always be analyzed in its full context when literal falsity is evaluated, and that relief remains available for an advertisement that is not literally false if it has misled, confused, or deceived the consuming public — a showing typically made through consumer surveys.

expectedJSON.body: Traditional passing off is selling one's own goods as those of another. Reverse passing off is the mirror image: selling another's goods as one's own. In Smith v. Montoro, 648 F.2d 602 (9th Cir. 1981), an actor alleged that a film distributor had removed his name from the credits and advertising for a film in which he had starred and substituted another actor's name. The district court dismissed the Lanham Act claim on the ground that the conduct was not the economic equivalent of palming off. The Ninth Circuit reversed, holding that a section 43(a) claim may rest on conduct economically equivalent to palming off, and describing reverse passing off as conduct that occurs when a person removes or obliterates the original trademark, without authorization, before reselling goods produced by someone else. The court distinguished two forms. Express reverse passing off occurs when the wrongdoer removes the name or trademark on another party's product and sells that product under a name the wrongdoer chooses. Implied reverse passing off occurs when the wrongdoer simply removes or obliterates the name of the manufacturer or source and sells the product unbranded. The court described the injury as both a misappropriation of another's talents and workmanship and a deprivation of the advertising value of the originator's name and of the goodwill that public knowledge of the true source would generate.

Dastar copied the series, made modifications, and sold the result as its own video set without crediting the original. The holders of rights connected with the original series sued under section 43(a), arguing that selling the copied material without acknowledging its source was a false designation of origin. The Supreme Court reversed the judgment against Dastar. It drew a line between two situations: a claim would undoubtedly have been sustained had Dastar bought finished videotapes from the authorized distributor and repackaged them as its own, but Dastar had instead copied a public-domain work and produced its own tapes. The consequence is that a failure to credit the creator of content that a defendant lawfully copied is not, without more, a violation of 15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(1)(A).

Section 43(a), the Court said, prohibits actions like trademark infringement that deceive consumers and impair a producer's goodwill; its illustration was one soft-drink company passing off its product as a competitor's, or reverse passing off the competitor's product as its own. Stover Seed Co., 108 F.3d 1134 (9th Cir. 1997), a suit between competing sellers of turfgrass seed over advertisements comparing growth rates. The elements are a false statement of fact by the defendant in a commercial advertisement about its own or another's product; a statement that actually deceived or has the tendency to deceive a substantial segment of its audience; materiality, in that the deception is likely to influence the purchasing decision; entry of the false statement into interstate commerce caused by the defendant; and injury to the plaintiff, or likely injury, either by direct diversion of sales or by a lessening of the goodwill associated with the plaintiff's products. Falsity may be shown in either of two ways: that the statement was literally false, on its face or by necessary implication, or that it was literally true but likely to mislead or confuse consumers. The court added that an advertising claim must always be analyzed in its full context when literal falsity is evaluated, and that relief remains available for an advertisement that is not literally false if it has misled, confused, or deceived the consuming public — a showing typically made through consumer surveys.

expectedJSON.body: Two sections of the Lanham Act supply the remedies for a violation of 15 U.S.C. § 1125(a). Section 1116(a) gives the courts power to grant injunctions according to the principles of equity and on terms the court deems reasonable, both to prevent violation of a registrant's rights and to prevent a violation under subsection (a), (c), or (d) of section 1125. That subsection also provides a rebuttable presumption of irreparable harm: on a finding of a violation for a permanent injunction, or on a finding of likelihood of success on the merits for a preliminary injunction or temporary restraining order. Section 1117(a) governs money: once a violation under section 1125(a) is established, the plaintiff is entitled, subject to the principles of equity, to recover the defendant's profits, any damages sustained, and the costs of the action; in assessing profits the plaintiff need prove only the defendant's sales, while the defendant must prove any claimed cost or deduction. The court may enter judgment for a sum above actual damages, not exceeding three times that amount, according to the circumstances of the case, and the statute states that such a sum is compensation and not a penalty. Attorney's fees are available only in exceptional cases, where the court may award reasonable fees to the prevailing party.

Business and Professions Code section 17200 defines unfair competition to mean and include any unlawful, unfair, or fraudulent business act or practice and unfair, deceptive, untrue, or misleading advertising, and it incorporates any act prohibited by the false advertising chapter that begins at section 17500. Section 17500 makes it unlawful for a person, firm, corporation, or association, or an employee, with intent to dispose of property or perform services or to induce the public to enter into an obligation, to disseminate before the public a statement concerning the property or services, or a circumstance connected with their proposed performance or disposition, that is untrue or misleading and that is known, or by the exercise of reasonable care should be known, to be untrue or misleading; the section covers dissemination including over the Internet and makes a violation a misdemeanor. Section 17204 identifies who may prosecute an action for relief under the unfair competition chapter: the Attorney General, a district attorney, specified county counsel and city attorneys, and a person who has suffered injury in fact and has lost money or property as a result of the unfair competition.
